question: Which of the following rivers is NOT mentioned in Rigveda?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Krishna**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Rigveda is the oldest of the four Vedas and is a primary source of early Indian history, focusing on hymns, rituals, and nature worship.
 
• Rivers like Saraswati, Sindhu (Indus), and Yamuna are prominently mentioned in the Rigveda as sacred rivers with vital cultural and religious significance.
 
• The Rigveda praises the Sindhu (Indus) as a mighty river, referring to it as the lifeblood of the ancient Vedic civilization.
 
• The Saraswati River, often described as a divine and mythical river, is extensively referenced in the Rigveda, symbolizing fertility and prosperity.
 
• Krishna, a river in southern India, is not mentioned in the Rigveda, as the focus of the text is primarily on rivers in the northwestern and northern regions of the Indian subcontinent.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Geographical Context of the Rigveda:** The hymns of the Rigveda were composed in the Sapta Sindhu (land of seven rivers) region, which includes the modern-day areas of Punjab and Haryana.
 
• **Important Rivers in the Rigveda:** The Rigveda mentions rivers like Saraswati, Sindhu (Indus), Ganga, Yamuna, and others, emphasizing their significance in agriculture, rituals, and trade.
 
• **Saraswati River:** The Saraswati River, often considered mythical, is described as flowing between the Yamuna and Sutlej rivers. It is central to Vedic cosmology and is regarded as a sacred river.
 
• **Absence of Southern Rivers:** Rivers like Krishna, Godavari, and Kaveri, located in southern India, are not mentioned in the Rigveda, as the Vedic civilization primarily flourished in northern and northwestern India during its composition.
 
• **Later Textual Developments:** The southern rivers gained prominence in later texts like the Mahabharata, Ramayana, and Puranas, reflecting the geographic expansion of Vedic culture over time.
